subject: Coffee & Tea
title: The Decline of London Coffeehouses
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Decline of London Coffeehouses usable.

hook.text: By the mid-1700s, London's coffeehouses were disappearing. Tea had conquered Britain, and private clubs took over.

buildup.text: Wealthy patrons moved to exclusive gentlemen's clubs—like White's and Boodle's—leaving coffeehouses to the masses.

discovery.text: Tea imports from China skyrocketed. By 1750, Britons drank more tea than coffee—a shift that never reversed.

twist.text: The East India Company lobbied for tea because it controlled Asian trade routes. Commerce shaped a nation's taste.

climax.text: London's vibrant coffeehouse culture faded in a few decades. The institutions it birthed—Lloyd's, the Stock Exchange—lived on.

punchline.text: The coffeehouses died. But everything they created still stands.

quiz.question: Why did London coffeehouses decline in the 1700s?
options: Tea replaced coffee, and wealthy patrons moved to private clubs

details.summary: London's coffeehouse era faded in the mid-1700s as tea became Britain's preferred drink and private gentlemen's clubs absorbed the upper-class clientele. Coffeehouses evolved into specialized institutions like Lloyd's and the Stock Exchange, or simply became tea rooms and taverns.
details.whyItMatters: The decline shows how shifting tastes and social structures transform cultural institutions. The coffeehouse's functions survived in other forms rather than disappearing.
takeaways: Tea overtook coffee as Britain's favorite drink by the 1750s
Private clubs absorbed wealthy coffeehouse patrons
Many coffeehouses evolved into financial institutions

faq.question: Why did tea replace coffee in Britain?
faq.answer: The East India Company made tea cheaply available from its colonies. Tea was easier to prepare at home, could be sweetened with sugar from Caribbean plantations, and was marketed as a domestic family beverage. Coffee remained a coffeehouse drink while tea became the drink of the home.

faq.question: Did coffeehouses disappear entirely from London?
faq.answer: Not entirely, but they lost their central cultural role. Some survived for decades as specialty establishments. The coffeehouse concept returned in the 20th century with espresso bars and again with third-wave specialty cafes, though in very different forms.
